sources: NHS.uk heart failure: call 999 for severe difficulty breathing (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heart-failure/); CTAS respiratory distress severe = level 1 (CTAS Participant Manual 2013)

NHS.uk: call 999 (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/anaphylaxis/); NHS Pathways Dx0113 anaphylaxis = Category 2 ambulance; CTAS allergic reaction with airway compromise = level 1 (Ontario Prehospital CTAS Guide 2016)

NHS.uk: Ebola is an emergency and needs to be treated quickly; call 111 and stay home for isolation (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ebola/); WHO: seeking early care can be lifesaving (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/ebola-disease)

Cleveland Clinic: call 911 if still unable to breathe or speak after the episode (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/22406-laryngospasm); CTAS sore throat with stridor = level 2 (CTAS Quick Look 2025); typical episode self-terminates (docs/ddxplus-severity-validation.md)

NHS.uk heart attack: call 999 (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heart-attack/); NHS Pathways Dx0112 ACS = Category 2 ambulance; CTAS chest pain with cardiac features = level 2, ECG within 15 min (Bullard 2017 CJEM doi:10.1017/cem.2017.365)

CTAS gait disturbance with extrapyramidal symptoms = level 2 (CTAS Quick Look 2025); laryngeal dystonia can obstruct the airway, same-day anticholinergic reverses it (PMID 38185029 via docs/ddxplus-severity-validation.md)

Cleveland Clinic: medical emergency, call 911 for severe chest pain after vomiting (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/22898-boerhaave-syndrome); CTAS vomiting blood active = level 2 (Ontario Prehospital CTAS Guide 2016); mortality 30% (Allaway 2021 via docs/ddxplus-severity-validation.md)

NHS.uk: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if you think your child has croup, 999 if struggling to breathe (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/croup/); CTAS paediatric stridor audible at rest = level 3, marked stridor = level 2 (CTAS Participant Manual 2013)
NHS.uk: call 999 if you think you or your child may have epiglottitis (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/epiglottitis/); CTAS sore throat with drooling or stridor = level 2 (CTAS Quick Look 2025)

NHS.uk: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if you think you have GBS, 999 for swallowing or facial weakness (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/guillain-barre-syndrome/); 14-22% ventilated in the first week (Walgaard 2010 via docs/ddxplus-severity-validation.md)

BHF: contact your doctor straightaway or call 111, 999 if chest pain lasts more than 15 min (https://www.bhf.org.uk/informationsupport/conditions/myocarditis); CTAS chest pain with cardiac features = level 2 (Bullard 2017)

CTAS palpitations, acute onset or ongoing = level 3 (CTAS Quick Look 2025); NHS.uk: 999 if the episode lasts longer than usual or comes with breathlessness, chest pain or faintness (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/supraventricular-tachycardia-svt/)

NHS.uk: call 999 or go to A&E for severe difficulty breathing, chest pain, very fast heartbeat or collapse (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/pulmonary-embolism/); NICE NG158 imaging within 4 h or interim anticoagulation (via docs/ddxplus-severity-validation.md)

CDC Yellow Book: responds to antihistamines, resolves within 12 h, rarely respiratory compromise or hypotension (https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/environmental-hazards-risks/food-poisoning-from-marine-toxins.html); CTAS paediatric allergic reaction moderate = level 3 (Ontario Prehospital CTAS Guide 2016)

CTAS sharp localized pleuritic pain = level 3, moderate shortness of breath = level 2 (Beveridge 1998 CTAS v16; CTAS Participant Manual 2013); Leicester NHS leaflet: 999 or ED if symptoms return (https://yourhealth.leicestershospitals.nhs.uk/library/renal-respiratory-cardiovascular-rrcv/respiratory-1/61-pneumothorax-a-collapsed-lung/file); BTS 2023 ED assessment before ambulatory care (via docs/ddxplus-severity-validation.md)

NHS.uk angina: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for chest pain or other angina symptoms that come and go; 999 if pain does not stop at rest (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/angina/); NICE CG95 rapid access chest pain clinic within 2 weeks after GP assessment (via docs/ddxplus-severity-validation.md)

NHS.uk angina: call 999 if chest pain does not stop after a few minutes of rest or angina medicine (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/angina/); ESC 2023 ACS pathway (via docs/ddxplus-severity-validation.md)

NICE NG115 Table 7: treat at home if breathlessness mild and general condition good, in hospital if severe, deteriorating, cyanosed or confused (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng115); NHS.uk bronchitis: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for shortness of breath or a chronic condition (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/bronchitis/); CTAS shortness of breath mild = level 3 (CTAS Participant Manual 2013)

NICE NG196 1.1.1-1.1.2: pulse palpation then 12-lead ECG for suspected AF; 1.8.1: emergency cardioversion only for life-threatening haemodynamic instability (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196); NHS.uk: see a GP, 999 with chest pain, breathlessness or fainting (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/atrial-fibrillation/); CTAS palpitations recent and now asymptomatic = level 4 (CTAS Quick Look 2025)

NHS.uk: see a GP for a cough lasting more than 3 weeks; urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for a rapidly worsening cough, blood-flecked sputum or breathlessness (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/bronchiectasis/)

sources: NHS.uk: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for a worsening cold, feeding much less or fever; 999 for breathing difficulty, pauses in breathing or blue colour (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/bronchiolitis/); NICE NG9 1.2.1 immediate 999 referral for apnoea, severe distress or cyanosis; 1.3.3 risk factors: under 3 months, prematurity, congenital heart disease, chronic lung disease (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng9)

modifiers: E_101 hospitalised for asthma in the past year or E_46 two or more attacks in a year -> 1 (BTS/SIGN near-fatal asthma risk factors, via docs/ddxplus-severity-validation.md)
sources: NHS.uk asthma attack: 999 if not better after the maximum reliever dose or feeling worse; urgent GP appointment after recovery (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/asthma/asthma-attack/); CTAS shortness of breath asthmatic mild = level 3, moderate = level 2 (CTAS Quick Look 2025)
CDC: antiparasitic treatment for all acute cases; chronic cases treated by age band; no time-critical disposition (https://www.cdc.gov/chagas/hcp/clinical-care/index.html)

NTS U3 definition includes humane reasons such as severe pain (Werkwijze NTS April 2025, https://www.de-nts.nl/app/uploads/2025/05/Werkwijze-NTS-april_25.pdf); NHS.uk: see a GP if you think you might have cluster headaches, 999 for new ptosis or unequal pupils (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/cluster-headaches/); CTAS chronic or recurring headache = level 5, sudden severe = level 2 (CTAS Quick Look 2025; Participant Manual 2013)
NHS.uk: pharmacist or self-care first, see a GP if not helping or heartburn most days (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/heartburn-and-acid-reflux/)

NHS.uk: go to a sexual health clinic or see a GP (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hiv-and-aids/); CDC: start treatment as soon as possible after diagnosis (https://www.cdc.gov/hivnexus/hcp/diagnosis-testing/index.html)

modifiers: age >= 65, or E_167 pregnancy, or chronic disease (E_123/E_31 COPD, E_124 asthma, E_106 heart failure, E_69 diabetes, E_113 CKD, E_126 cirrhosis), or immunosuppression (E_227, E_2 HIV, E_34 cancer) -> 3 (NHS.uk urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 rung; CDC antivirals as soon as possible for higher-risk groups)
sources: NHS.uk flu: self-care; urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if 65 or over, pregnant, long-term condition, weakened immunity, very unwell or not improving after 7 days (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/flu/); CDC antiviral summary for clinicians (https://www.cdc.gov/flu/hcp/antivirals/summary-clinicians.html)
NHS.uk: see a GP if you think you have a hernia; NHS 111 if painful with vomiting, bloating or fever (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/hernia/)
NHS.uk: see a GP for long-lasting or worrying symptoms; urgent hospital treatment if breathing or swallowing suddenly worsens (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/myasthenia-gravis/)

NICE NG12 1.2.4: suspected cancer pathway referral within 2 weeks for jaundice at age 40 and over; 1.2.5: urgent CT within 2 weeks at age 60 and over with weight loss plus symptoms (https://docs.bvsalud.org/biblioref/2022/02/1355289/suspected-cancer-recognition-and-referral-pdf-1837268071621.pdf)

modifiers: age >= 65, or chronic lung disease (E_123/E_31), or heart failure (E_106), or immunosuppression (E_227, E_2, E_34) -> 2 (NHS.uk: may need hospital treatment if over 65 or with cardiovascular or chronic lung disease; CRB-65 age point, Lim 2003 via docs/ddxplus-severity-validation.md; NTS risk-group rule raises urgency for chronic disease and immunosuppression)
sources: NHS.uk pneumonia: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for cough with chest pain or shortness of breath; 999 if struggling to breathe or confused (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/pneumonia/); NTS Werkwijze April 2025 risk-group rule (https://www.de-nts.nl/app/uploads/2025/05/Werkwijze-NTS-april_25.pdf)

NICE NG12 1.1.1: suspected cancer pathway referral within 2 weeks; 1.1.2: urgent chest X-ray within 2 weeks at age 40 and over with 2 or more symptoms, or 1 symptom if ever smoked (NG12 PDF mirror as above); NHS.uk: see a GP for a cough over 3 weeks, urgent if coughing up blood (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lung-cancer/symptoms/)
NHS.uk broken or bruised ribs: self-care, ribs heal in 2-6 weeks; urgent GP or 111 only if not improving or with fever (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/broken-or-bruised-ribs/)

NHS.uk: see a GP for a cough over 3 weeks, night sweats or weight loss; urgent if coughing up blood (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/tuberculosis-tb/); NICE NG33 urgent referral to a TB service (via docs/ddxplus-severity-validation.md)
NHS.uk: self-care or pharmacist, resolves in 1-2 weeks; 111 if very painful or difficult to swallow (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/laryngitis/)

modifiers: E_227 immunosuppression, E_69 diabetes, E_106 heart failure, E_123/E_31 COPD, E_113 CKD -> 3 (NHS.uk urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 rung for chronic disease or weakened immunity; NTS risk-group rule)
sources: NHS.uk ear infections: pharmacist first for ages 1-17; see a GP under 12 months or if not improving after 3 days; urgent GP or 111 if very unwell, immunosuppressed or with diabetes, heart, lung, kidney or neurological disease (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ear-infections/)

modifiers: E_227 immunosuppression -> 3 (NHS.uk urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 rung)
sources: NHS.uk sinusitis: self-care then pharmacist; see a GP after 3 weeks; urgent GP or 111 if very unwell or immunosuppressed (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sinusitis-sinus-infection/)
NHS.uk allergic rhinitis: can often be treated without seeing a GP (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/allergic-rhinitis/); CTAS nasal congestion or hay fever = level 5 (CTAS Quick Look 2025)
NHS.uk iron deficiency anaemia: non-urgent advice, see a GP (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/iron-deficiency-anaemia/)

sources: NHS.uk bronchitis: self-care, usually better in 3 weeks; urgent GP or 111 if over 65, pregnant, chronic disease, immunosuppressed, cough over 3 weeks or short of breath; 999 if struggling to breathe (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/bronchitis/); CTAS URTI, appears well, no fever = level 5 (CTAS Quick Look 2025)

NHS.uk oedema: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if one leg is swollen without a known cause or the area is red or hot; 999 with breathlessness or chest pain (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/oedema/); CTAS leg swelling above the ankles = level 4, with fever = level 2 (CTAS Quick Look 2025)

NHS.uk pericarditis: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for sharp chest pain worse on breathing in or lying down; 999 for crushing pain over 15 min (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/pericarditis/); ESC 2015 same-day risk stratification (via docs/ddxplus-severity-validation.md); CTAS chest pain non-cardiac, acute onset and ongoing = level 3 (Ontario Prehospital CTAS Guide 2016)
NHS.uk lupus: see a GP if you often get symptoms of lupus (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/lupus/)
NHS.uk sarcoidosis page gives no urgent disposition (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sarcoidosis/); routine GP assessment

sources: NHS.uk sore throat: self-care or pharmacist; GP if not better after a week; urgent 111 for high temperature or weakened immunity; 999 for drooling or stridor (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sore-throat/); CTAS sore throat or URI, not severe, temperature under 39 C = level 5 (Beveridge 1998 CTAS v16)

NHS.uk sinusitis: a GP may refer to ENT after 3 months (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/sinusitis-sinus-infection/)
NHS.uk panic disorder: self-care during an attack, see a GP for panic disorder symptoms (https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/conditions/panic-disorder/)
